headline: High risk of cascading errors and capability conflict; prompt-injection and leakage are lower but non-zero due to shared MCP/egress surfaces.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can use MCP and stdin/stdout, so if its outputs are routed into Agent B’s OIDC/ForwardAuth workflows or shared files, instruction-like content could be misread. Agent B has no browser or subprocesses, which limits exploitability, but the shared integration surface is enough to make injection plausible.
conditions: IF Agent A output is copied into a shared workspace or MCP channel that Agent B parses as instructions
IF Agent B consumes untrusted text from Agent A without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic parsing of Agent A text as commands
Add provenance tags to all A→B messages
Route A output through a human review step
Restrict MCP channels to read-only payloads
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and schema validation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and secrets (Ed25519 signatures), while Agent B has broad network egress but no documented data classes touched. The pair does not show a shared workspace or authenticated principal, so leakage is possible mainly through operator-mediated transfer or misrouted logs, not by default.
conditions: IF Agent A logs secrets or prompts into a location Agent B can read
IF the operator forwards A’s outputs into B’s network-facing workflows
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces
Redact secrets before any handoff
Disable verbose logging on both agents
Review outbound destinations for B
requires-engineering: add per-field data-loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; Agent B exposes OIDC/OAuth and ForwardAuth APIs. Even without a shared filesystem, overlapping authority over mutable auth or repo-adjacent resources can create write conflicts if orchestrated together, and the profiles do not show locking or coordination.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same git repository or auth configuration
IF the orchestrator allows concurrent writes without locks
mitigations: Serialize writes to shared resources
Assign separate repositories or tenants
Disable concurrent runs on the same target
Add a lock file or lease mechanism
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate and transform repository/task content, and Agent B exposes authentication/authorization APIs that may act on upstream inputs. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, a mistaken A result can cascade into access-control or routing errors. No verification step is documented, so the safer choice is the higher severity.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes Agent A output without independent validation
IF A’s generated configuration or claims are used to update auth policy
mitigations: Require explicit validation before B acts
Add checksum or schema checks on A outputs
Use a human approval gate for auth changes
Log and diff all A→B handoffs
requires-engineering: add policy simulation before enforcement

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. The only concrete compliance-relevant surface is Agent B’s OIDC/ForwardAuth role and Agent A’s handling of prompts and repository metadata, so the pair presents a small but plausible policy-gap risk rather than a documented breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through Agent B without a matching policy
IF retention or logging settings differ across the two deployments
mitigations: Confirm both deployments’ retention settings
Avoid sending regulated data through B
Document data-flow boundaries
Review access logs after first run
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
